Patient: I'm 28 years old and female. I came in because my blood pressure was really high, and I felt light-headed and almost fell yesterday. My boyfriend caught me and we went straight to the ER.
Doctor: Could you please confirm your current blood pressure reading and any medications you are taking?
Patient: My blood pressure was really high in the ER, like almost 200, but I don't have the exact number now. I'm taking lisinopril, which I've been on for a while.
Doctor: Have you experienced any chest pain, palpitations, or visual disturbances alongside the hypertension?
Patient: No, I haven't had chest pain or palpitations, and I didn't have any visual disturbances. The main things were the light-headedness and the feeling like I was going to fall. It was pretty scary, but my boyfriend was there to catch me.
Doctor: Has there been a family history of hypertension, migraines, or neurological conditions such as seizures or stroke? Have you experienced similar episodes in the past?
Patient: I don't have a family history of hypertension, migraines, or neurological conditions. I haven't had similar episodes before, but my blood pressure has been running high once a month or so, usually when I'm traveling for work and not eating as well.
Doctor: Could you describe any neurological symptoms you experienced during the episode, such as vision changes, speech difficulties, weakness, or numbness?
Patient: No, I didn't experience any vision changes, speech difficulties, weakness, or numbness during the episode. The main thing was just feeling light-headed and like I was going to fall. It was pretty scary, but my boyfriend was there to catch me.
Doctor: Could you provide the exact blood pressure reading from the ER and any results from previous blood pressure monitoring or ambulatory blood pressure measurements?
Patient: I don't have the exact blood pressure reading from the ER, but it was really high, like almost 200. I don't have any results from previous blood pressure monitoring or ambulatory measurements, but I do check it sometimes when I'm home, though not as consistently as I should.
Doctor: Could you describe any other symptoms you experience during these episodes, such as chest pain, palpitations, or visual disturbances? Additionally, have you had any imaging studies like a head CT, MRI, or echocardiogram to evaluate for secondary causes of hypertension or neurological involvement?
Patient: I don't have any other symptoms during these episodes besides the light-headedness and feeling like I'm going to fall. I haven't had any imaging studies like a head CT, MRI, or echocardiogram to evaluate for secondary causes of hypertension or neurological involvement.
Doctor: Have you undergone any renal function tests, such as serum creatinine, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), or urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, to evaluate for renal causes of secondary hypertension?
Patient: I don't have any information about renal function tests like serum creatinine, eGFR, or urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio. That information isn't available to me.
Doctor: Have you experienced any other symptoms during these episodes, such as chest pain, palpitations, visual changes, or headaches?
Patient: I did have a headache during the episode, but no chest pain, palpitations, or visual changes. The headache was pretty intense, but it went away after I got to the ER.
Doctor: Have you undergone any endocrine evaluations, such as a plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio, cortisol levels, or imaging of the adrenal glands, to rule out secondary causes of hypertension?
Patient: No, I haven't had any endocrine evaluations like a plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio, cortisol levels, or imaging of the adrenal glands. That information isn't available to me.
Doctor: Could you please provide the results of your most recent physical examination, particularly focusing on cardiovascular and neurological findings?
Patient: I don't have the results of my most recent physical examination, but the doctor mentioned during the visit that my blood pressure was still a little elevated. He listened to my heart and found a slight murmur, and he said my lungs were clear. He also noted some trace pitting edema in my lower extremities. That's all I know about the exam.
Doctor: Could you provide the exact blood pressure reading recorded in the ER during the episode, as well as the results of your most recent serum creatinine, eGFR, and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio tests?
Patient: I don't have the exact blood pressure reading from the ER, and I don't have the results of serum creatinine, eGFR, or urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio tests. That information isn't available to me.
Doctor: Have you undergone any imaging studies such as an echocardiogram, head CT, or MRI to evaluate for potential neurological or cardiac causes of your symptoms?
Patient: I don't have the results of imaging studies like an echocardiogram, head CT, or MRI. That information isn't available to me.
Doctor: Could you provide the exact blood pressure reading from the ER and confirm whether an echocardiogram has been performed to evaluate the heart murmur and assess for structural heart disease?
Patient: I don't have the exact blood pressure reading from the ER, but I was told that it was really high, almost 200. As for the echocardiogram, the doctor showed me the results from a few months ago, which showed that I have a slightly leaky heart valve, but nothing else was found.
Doctor: Could you provide the exact blood pressure reading from the ER and confirm if any endocrine evaluations, such as plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio, cortisol levels, or adrenal imaging, have been performed?
Patient: I don't have the exact blood pressure reading from the ER, but I was told it was really high, almost 200. As for endocrine evaluations like plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio, cortisol levels, or adrenal imaging, that information isn't available to me.
